title: Current Electricity
subject: Physics
subtitle: Class 12 HSC & MHT-CET • Rapid Revision Deck

cards.q: State Kirchhoff's First Law (Current Law / Junction Rule) and its conservation basis.
cards.a:
The algebraic sum of currents meeting at any electrical junction is zero: ∑ I = 0 (Current entering junction = Current leaving junction).
Conservation basis: Law of Conservation of CHARGE.
cards.hint: Sign convention: Currents entering the junction are positive; currents leaving are negative.

cards.q: State Kirchhoff's Second Law (Voltage Law / Loop Rule) and its conservation basis.
cards.a:
In any closed electrical loop, the algebraic sum of changes in potential (product of current and resistance plus EMFs) is zero: ∑ (I R) + ∑ E = 0.
Conservation basis: Law of Conservation of ENERGY.
cards.hint: Crucial Board distinction: KCL = Conservation of Charge; KVL = Conservation of Energy.

cards.q: Wheatstone's Bridge: Balancing condition and galvanometer current?
cards.a:
Balancing condition: P / Q = R / S.
At balance point, potential at points B and D is equal (V_B = V_D), so galvanometer current is ZERO (I_g = 0).
cards.hint: The position of battery and galvanometer can be interchanged without affecting the balance condition.

cards.q: Condition for Maximum Sensitivity of a Wheatstone's Bridge?
cards.a: The bridge is most sensitive when all four resistances are approximately of the same order of magnitude (P ≈ Q ≈ R ≈ S).
cards.hint: If one arm is very large and another very small, sensitivity drops significantly.

cards.q: Meter Bridge (Slide Wire Bridge): Working formula to determine unknown resistance X?
cards.a: X / R = l_X / l_R = l_X / (100 - l_X) ⇒ X = R · [ l_X / (100 - l_X) ], where l_X is balancing length in cm.
cards.hint: Balancing length should ideally be obtained near the center (between 40 cm and 60 cm) to minimize fractional errors.

cards.q: Kelvin's Method in Meter Bridge: Purpose and procedure?
cards.a:
Used to determine the resistance of a GALVANOMETER (G) itself.
The galvanometer is connected in one gap, and a variable jockey is used to find a point on the wire where galvanometer shows the SAME deflection with jockey tapped or open.
cards.hint: Null deflection method where galvanometer itself acts as the detector without any auxiliary detector!

cards.q: State the Principle of Potentiometer.
cards.a: The potential difference between any two points of a uniform wire carrying steady current is directly proportional to the length of wire between those points: V ∝ l ⇒ V = K · l, where K = V/L is Potential Gradient.
cards.hint: SI unit of Potential Gradient K is V/m. Lower potential gradient means higher sensitivity.

cards.q: Comparison of EMF of two cells using Potentiometer: Individual vs Sum and Difference methods?
cards.a:
Individual Method: E₁ / E₂ = l₁ / l₂
Sum and Difference Method: (E₁ + E₂) / (E₁ - E₂) = l₁ / l₂ ⇒ E₁ / E₂ = (l₁ + l₂) / (l₁ - l₂).
cards.hint: Sum method: cells assist each other (E₁ + E₂); difference method: cells oppose each other (E₁ - E₂).

cards.q: Formula to determine Internal Resistance r of a cell using Potentiometer?
cards.a: r = R · [ (l₁ - l₂) / l₂ ] = R · [ (l₁ / l₂) - 1 ], where l₁ is open circuit balancing length (EMF E) and l₂ is closed circuit balancing length across shunt resistance R (terminal PD V).
cards.hint: l₁ is always greater than l₂ because terminal voltage V < EMF E.

cards.q: Why is a Potentiometer preferred over a Voltmeter for measuring EMF?
cards.a: A potentiometer draws ZERO current from the source at the null balance point (infinite effective internal resistance). A voltmeter always draws some current, measuring terminal voltage V < E.
cards.hint: A potentiometer acts as an ideal infinite-resistance voltmeter.

cards.q: How to increase the sensitivity of a Potentiometer?
cards.a:
Decrease its potential gradient K = V/L by:
1. Increasing the length of potentiometer wire L (using 8-10 wire potentiometers).
2. Decreasing the primary circuit current by adding resistance (rheostat).
cards.hint: Lower K means smaller potential differences correspond to larger, easily measurable balancing lengths.

cards.q: Conversion of Galvanometer (resistance G) into an Ammeter (range 0 to I)?
cards.a:
Connect a low resistance SHUNT (S) in PARALLEL with the galvanometer:
S = [ I_g / (I - I_g) ] · G = G / (n - 1), where n = I / I_g is multiplying factor.
cards.hint: Effective resistance of ammeter: R_A = (G · S) / (G + S) ≈ S (very small; ideal ammeter resistance is 0).

cards.q: Conversion of Galvanometer (resistance G) into a Voltmeter (range 0 to V)?
cards.a:
Connect a high resistance R_s in SERIES with the galvanometer:
R_s = (V / I_g) - G = G (n - 1), where n = V / V_g is multiplying factor (V_g = I_g G).
cards.hint: Effective resistance of voltmeter: R_V = G + R_s (very large; ideal voltmeter resistance is ∞).

cards.q: Drift Velocity v_d, Relaxation time τ, and Current I relation?
cards.a:
v_d = e E τ / m = e V τ / (m L).
Current: I = n A e v_d = n A e² E τ / m.
Current density: J = I / A = n e v_d = σ E.
cards.hint: Drift velocity in metals is very small (~10⁻⁴ m/s = 0.1 mm/s), yet electric signals travel near speed of light!

cards.q: Temperature coefficient of resistance α: Formula and units?
cards.a:
R_T = R₀ (1 + α ΔT) ⇒ α = (R_T - R₀) / (R₀ · ΔT).
SI unit of α: per kelvin (K⁻¹) or per °C (°C⁻¹).
cards.hint:
For metals/conductors: α > 0 (resistance increases with temperature).
For semiconductors and insulators: α < 0 (resistance decreases with temperature).

cards.q: Stretching a wire: If length of a wire of resistance R is stretched by n times, what is the new resistance?
cards.a:
R' = n² · R.
If stretched by x% (small elongation < 5%): ΔR / R ≈ 2 · (ΔL / L) = 2x%.
cards.hint: Volume is constant: V = A · L = constant ⇒ If L becomes n L, area becomes A / n ⇒ R' = ρ (n L) / (A / n) = n² R.

cards.q: Terminal Potential Difference V of a cell of EMF E and internal resistance r?
cards.a:
During Discharging: V = E - I r  (V < E)
During Charging: V = E + I r  (V > E)
On Open Circuit (I = 0): V = E
Short Circuit Current (R = 0): I_sc = E / r (V = 0).
cards.hint: Terminal voltage exceeds EMF ONLY when the cell is being charged by an external source!

cards.q: Maximum Power Transfer Theorem for a DC circuit?
cards.a:
Power delivered to an external load resistance R by a cell of EMF E and internal resistance r is MAXIMUM when: R = r (load resistance equals internal resistance).
Maximum Power: P_max = E² / (4 r).
cards.hint: When R = r, efficiency is 50% (half energy is dissipated internally in the cell).

cards.q: Grouping of n identical cells (each EMF E, internal resistance r)?
cards.a:
Series: E_eq = n E, r_eq = n r ⇒ I = n E / (R + n r).
Parallel: E_eq = E, r_eq = r / n ⇒ I = E / (R + r / n).
Mixed grouping (m rows of n cells): I = n E / [ R + (n r / m) ]. Maximum current when R = n r / m.
cards.hint: Series grouping gives maximum current when external R ≫ n r; parallel when external R ≪ r / n.

cards.q: What is Thermoelectricity (Seebeck Effect and Peltier Effect)?
cards.a:
Seebeck Effect: Production of an electric current in a closed loop of two dissimilar metals when their junctions are maintained at different temperatures (heat → electricity).
Peltier Effect: Absorption or evolution of heat at a junction of two dissimilar metals when an electric current passes through it (electricity → heat; reverse of Seebeck).
cards.hint: Neutral temperature T_n is independent of cold junction: T_n = (T_c + T_i) / 2, where T_i is inversion temperature.

cards.q: Heating effect of electric current (Joule's Law)?
cards.a:
H = I² R t = V I t = (V² / R) t  (in Joules).
Electric Power: P = I² R = V I = V² / R (in Watts).
cards.hint: In series, P ∝ R (higher resistance glows brighter); in parallel, P ∝ 1/R (lower resistance glows brighter).

cards.q: Two electric bulbs rated 220 V, 40 W and 220 V, 100 W: Which glows brighter in Series vs Parallel?
cards.a:
Resistance: R = V² / P ⇒ R_40 > R_100 (40 W bulb has higher resistance).
In Series (same current): P = I² R ⇒ 40 W bulb glows BRIGHTER.
In Parallel (same voltage): P = V² / R ⇒ 100 W bulb glows BRIGHTER.
cards.hint: Favorite trap! The lower wattage bulb glows brighter in series connection.

cards.q: End resistance error in Meter Bridge and how to eliminate it?
cards.a:
Caused by non-zero resistance of metallic copper strips and contact soldering points.
Elimination: Repeat the experiment by INTERCHANGING the positions of unknown resistance X and resistance box R in the two gaps and take average.
cards.hint: Interchanging gaps cancels out the end errors at both left and right ends.

cards.q: Superconductivity: Critical Temperature T_c and Meissner Effect?
cards.a:
Superconductivity: Resistance suddenly drops to EXACT ZERO at critical temperature T_c (e.g. Mercury at 4.2 K).
Meissner Effect: Complete expulsion of magnetic flux lines from the interior of a superconductor (perfect diamagnetism: χ = -1, μ_r = 0).
cards.hint: Once established, electric currents in a superconducting ring flow indefinitely without any potential difference.

cards.q: MHT-CET Trap: If an ideal ammeter is mistakenly connected in parallel across a circuit component, what happens?
cards.a: It creates a DEAD SHORT CIRCUIT! Because an ideal ammeter has zero resistance (R_A = 0), almost all current flows through the ammeter, which will burn out or blow the fuse.
cards.hint: Ammeters must ALWAYS be connected in series; voltmeters in parallel.
